items.prose: An anomaly detector watches a trading book. True anomalies occur on 2% of days. The detector catches 85% of them and false-alarms on 3% of normal days.
items.question: The detector fires today. What is the chance of a true anomaly? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two paths that end in an alarm.

byKey.inverse: That is the chance an anomaly is caught. You want the chance an alarm is an anomaly.
byKey.joint: That is anomaly and alarm together. Divide by every alarm.
byKey.base: That is the base rate. The alarm should raise it.

explain.text: Anomaly and alarm: $0.02 \times 0.85 = 0.017$. Normal and alarm: $0.98 \times 0.03 = 0.0294$. Under 37% of alarms are real.

items.prose: A rare event has prior probability 1%.
items.question: How large must a single piece of evidence's likelihood ratio be to lift it to at least 50%?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work in odds: 50% is odds of 1.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.01 to reach 0.5. Odds, not probabilities, are multiplied.
byKey.half: You aimed for odds of $\tfrac{1}{2}$. A probability of 50% is odds of 1.

explain.text: 1% is odds of $\tfrac{1}{99}$ and 50% is odds of 1. The ratio must be at least 99: very strong evidence for a rare event.

items.prose: A condition has prior 5%. Test A catches 95% of cases and false-alarms on 10% of healthy people. Test B catches 80% and false-alarms on 2%. A is positive; B, run independently, is negative.
items.question: What is the chance of the condition now? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance after A positive, B negative

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the prior odds by A's positive ratio and B's negative ratio.

byKey.a-only: That uses test A alone. B's negative is evidence too, with ratio $\tfrac{0.2}{0.98}$.
byKey.b-pos: You used B's positive ratio, 40. B came back negative: its ratio is $\tfrac{0.2}{0.98}$.
byKey.prior: That is where you started. Both results carry evidence.

explain.text: Prior odds are $\tfrac{1}{19}$. A positive multiplies them by $\tfrac{0.95}{0.1} = 9.5$, and B negative by $\tfrac{0.2}{0.98} \approx 0.204$. Odds $\tfrac{5}{49}$, so $p = \tfrac{5}{54} \approx 0.093$.

items.prose: A die is drawn from a box: 4-sided with chance 0.4, 6-sided 0.3, 8-sided 0.2, 12-sided 0.1. It is rolled once and shows 5.
items.question: Fill in the chance of each die after the roll.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each prior by the chance of a 5 on that die, then normalise.

byKey.r0c2: A 4-sided die cannot show 5, so it drops to 0.
byKey.r1c2: 6 sides: $0.3 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 0.05$, out of a total of $0.0833$.
byKey.r2c2: 8 sides: $0.2 \times \tfrac{1}{8} = 0.025$, out of $0.0833$. If you got $\tfrac{1}{3}$, you normalised the likelihoods without the priors.

explain.text: Products: 0, 0.05, 0.025 and 0.00833, adding to $\tfrac{1}{12}$. Normalised: 0, 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. The 4-sided die, the favourite before, is out.

items.prose: A condition $C$ has base rate $b$; a test has detection rate $h = P(+ \mid C)$ and false-positive rate $f = P(+ \mid \neg C)$. We derive $P(C \mid +)$ in terms of $b$, $h$ and $f$.
items.question: Put the lines in order. Start from Bayes' rule.

lines.text: $P(+) = P(+ \mid C)\,P(C) + P(+ \mid \neg C)\,P(\neg C)$: the law of total probability for the bottom
$P(C \mid +) = \dfrac{h\,b}{h\,b + f\,(1 - b)}$: substitute, with $P(\neg C) = 1 - b$
$P(C \mid +) = \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{f}{h} \cdot \dfrac{1 - b}{b}}$: divide top and bottom by $h\,b$

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.s2: Expanding the bottom comes after writing Bayes' rule.
byKey.s3: Substituting needs the expanded bottom first.
byKey.s4: Dividing by $h\,b$ needs the substituted form first.

explain.text: The last line shows the whole story: the posterior is small when $\tfrac{f}{h} \cdot \tfrac{1 - b}{b}$ is large. A rare condition makes $\tfrac{1 - b}{b}$ huge, so even a small $\tfrac{f}{h}$ cannot save it.

items.prose: A quant tests 200 strategies, of which 10 have a real edge. A backtest passes 80% of real strategies and 5% of noise. Passing strategies then face an independent out-of-sample test with the same two rates.
items.question: A strategy passes both. What is the chance it has a real edge? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a real edge after two passes

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each pass multiplies the odds by $\tfrac{0.8}{0.05} = 16$.

byKey.one: That is after the backtest alone: 8 real of 17.5 passes. The second test multiplies the odds by 16 again.
byKey.no-prior: You left out the prior odds, $\tfrac{10}{190}$. Most strategies are noise, and that has to count.
byKey.probs: That is $0.8 \times 0.8$, the chance a real strategy passes both. Turn it around with the base rate.

explain.text: Prior odds $\tfrac{10}{190} = \tfrac{1}{19}$. Each pass has ratio 16, so two give $\tfrac{256}{19}$ and $p \approx 0.93$. In counts: of 200, about 6.4 real and 0.475 noise strategies pass both.

items.title: Odds, base rates and repeated tests
items.prompt: Let $H$ be a hypothesis with $0 < P(H) < 1$ and $E$ evidence with $P(E) > 0$. (a) Derive the odds form of Bayes' rule: posterior odds $=$ likelihood ratio $\times$ prior odds. (b) A condition has base rate 1%; a test has detection rate 90% and false-positive rate 5%. Use (a) to find $P(H \mid +)$, and explain in one or two sentences why it is small. (c) Independent repeat tests with the same rates are run, all positive. How many are needed before $P(H \mid \text{all } +)$ exceeds 0.95? (d) Say what assumption (c) relies on, and give one way it could fail in practice.
items.model:
**(a)** Bayes' rule for $H$: $P(H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}$. For $\neg H$: $P(\neg H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid \neg H)\,P(\neg H)}{P(E)}$. Both are defined because $P(E) > 0$. Divide the first by the second; $P(E)$ cancels:
$$\frac{P(H \mid E)}{P(\neg H \mid E)} = \frac{P(E \mid H)}{P(E \mid \neg H)} \times \frac{P(H)}{P(\neg H)}.$$
The left side is the posterior odds. The first fraction is the likelihood ratio and the second is the prior odds.

**(b)** Prior odds $= \tfrac{0.01}{0.99} = \tfrac{1}{99}$. Likelihood ratio $= \tfrac{0.9}{0.05} = 18$. Posterior odds $= \tfrac{18}{99}$, so $P(H \mid +) = \tfrac{18}{117} = \tfrac{2}{13} \approx 0.154$. It is small because the healthy group is 99 times larger. Its 5% false positives (0.0495) outnumber the true positives (0.009).

**(c)** After $n$ positives the odds are $\tfrac{18^n}{99}$. We need $P > 0.95$, which is odds above 19, so $18^n > 1881$. That gives $n > \tfrac{\ln 1881}{\ln 18} \approx 2.61$, so $n = 3$. Check: $n = 2$ gives odds $\tfrac{324}{99} \approx 3.27$, $P \approx 0.766$; $n = 3$ gives $\tfrac{5832}{99} \approx 58.9$, $P \approx 0.983$.

**(d)** It assumes the tests err independently given $H$ and given $\neg H$, so their likelihood ratios multiply. It fails if the repeats use the same blood sample or machine. It also fails if a healthy person has a trait that fools every test. Then a second positive adds much less than a ratio of 18.

rubric.text: Writes Bayes' rule for $H$ and for $\neg H$ and notes $P(E) > 0$.
Divides the two so $P(E)$ cancels, and names posterior odds, likelihood ratio and prior odds.
Explains the small answer by the false positives from the much larger healthy group.
Sets up $\tfrac{18^n}{99} > 19$ and concludes $n = 3$, with a check of $n = 2$ and $n = 3$.
States conditional independence of the tests and gives a concrete way it fails.

items.prose: Two brokers both upgrade a stock to buy on the same morning. You learn both notes rest on the same management presentation, with no independent research.
items.question: How should you treat the two upgrades?

options.text: As not much more than one piece of evidence
As two independent signals: multiply the odds by both ratios
options.why: Both notes share one source. If the presentation misled one broker, it misled both.

options.text: As no evidence at all, since they agree
options.why: The presentation itself is real evidence. Only the second note adds little.

options.text: As evidence against, because agreement is suspicious
options.why: Shared sources weaken the second note; they do not turn it into evidence against.

feedback.correct: Shared sources make the second note largely redundant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the second note could have said something different.

explain.text: Multiplying ratios assumes each source errs independently. Here both notes inherit the same errors, so together they are worth little more than one. Counting both is double-counting.

items.prose: You give a stock a 60% chance of beating its earnings forecast. A supplier's warning is 3 times likelier if it will miss than if it will beat.
items.question: What is your new probability of a beat? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The ratio for a beat is $\tfrac{1}{3}$, since the warning favours a miss.

byKey.wrong-way: You multiplied the odds by 3. The warning favours a miss, so the ratio for a beat is $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
byKey.probs: You divided the probability 0.6 by 3. Divide the odds instead.
byKey.prior: That is where you started. The warning should lower it.

explain.text: Odds of a beat start at $\tfrac{0.6}{0.4} = 1.5$. The warning's ratio for a beat is $\tfrac{1}{3}$, giving odds 0.5 and $p = \tfrac{1}{3}$.

items.title: Two filters on a price feed
items.prompt:
Start from a blank page. A desk cleans a price feed. Each tick is bad, a data error, with chance $b$, and good otherwise, with $0 < b < 1$. Two filters check every tick. The jump filter flags a bad tick with chance $h_J$ and a good tick with chance $f_J$. The venue filter, which compares other exchanges, flags them with chances $h_V$ and $f_V$. Write $B$ for a bad tick, $G$ for a good one, and $J$ and $V$ for the two flags.

1. Starting from the multiplication rule, derive $P(B \mid J)$ in terms of $b$, $h_J$ and $f_J$. State any condition your steps need.
2. Both filters flag a tick. Derive $P(B \mid J \cap V)$ in terms of the five rates. Name, in plain words, the assumption about the filters that you need, and show where you use it.
3. Take $b = 0.02$, $h_J = 0.9$, $f_J = 0.06$, $h_V = 0.7$ and $f_V = 0.03$. Find $P(B \mid J)$ and $P(B \mid J \cap V)$ as fractions.
4. The desk then learns that on good ticks both filters read the same stale quote. A good tick is flagged by the venue filter only if the jump filter flags it too, and $f_V$ is still 0.03. On bad ticks the filters still flag independently. Find $P(B \mid J \cap V)$ now, and say which part of your assumption failed.

Optional, one more point: check one of your two-flag answers by a second route.
items.model:
**Setting.** $G$ is the complement of $B$, so $P(G) = 1 - b$, and both have positive chance since $0 < b < 1$. The four rates are chances given the kind of tick: $P(J \mid B) = h_J$, $P(J \mid G) = f_J$, $P(V \mid B) = h_V$ and $P(V \mid G) = f_V$.

**1. One flag.** The multiplication rule writes the chance of a bad, flagged tick through either event first:
$$\begin{aligned} P(B \cap J) &= P(J \mid B)\,P(B) \\ P(B \cap J) &= P(B \mid J)\,P(J). \end{aligned}$$
Both lines give the chance of the same event, so their right sides are equal. The second line defines $P(B \mid J)$ only when $P(J) > 0$, and then we may divide by $P(J)$:
$$P(B \mid J) = \frac{P(J \mid B)\,P(B)}{P(J)}.$$
Every tick is bad or good and not both, so $J$ splits into the disjoint events $J \cap B$ and $J \cap G$. Their chances add, and the multiplication rule gives each one:
$$\begin{aligned} P(J) &= P(J \mid B)\,P(B) + P(J \mid G)\,P(G) \\ &= h_J b + f_J(1 - b). \end{aligned}$$
So
$$P(B \mid J) = \frac{h_J b}{h_J b + f_J(1 - b)},$$
which needs $h_J b + f_J(1 - b) > 0$: the filter must flag some ticks.

**2. Two flags.** Part 1 used nothing about $J$ except $P(J) > 0$, so it holds with the event $J \cap V$ in place of $J$, when $P(J \cap V) > 0$. Write $N_B$ and $N_G$ for the bad and good paths into $J \cap V$:
$$\begin{aligned} N_B &= P(J \cap V \mid B)\,b, \\ N_G &= P(J \cap V \mid G)\,(1 - b), \\ P(B \mid J \cap V) &= \frac{N_B}{N_B + N_G}. \end{aligned}$$
To write $N_B$ and $N_G$ in the rates we need an assumption in two parts. On bad ticks the two filters flag independently, so $P(J \cap V \mid B) = h_J h_V$. On good ticks they also flag independently, so $P(J \cap V \mid G) = f_J f_V$. The first part turns $N_B$ into $h_J h_V b$, the top and the first term of the bottom. The second part turns $N_G$ into $f_J f_V(1 - b)$:
$$P(B \mid J \cap V) = \frac{h_J h_V b}{h_J h_V b + f_J f_V(1 - b)}.$$
Dividing $N_B$ by $N_G$ gives the same result in odds: the prior odds $\tfrac{b}{1 - b}$ times the two likelihood ratios $\tfrac{h_J}{f_J}$ and $\tfrac{h_V}{f_V}$.

**3. The numbers.** The two paths into $J$ are $0.02 \times 0.9 = 0.018$ and $0.98 \times 0.06 = 0.0588$, so $P(J) = 0.0768$. Then
$$P(B \mid J) = \frac{0.018}{0.0768} = \frac{15}{64} \approx 0.234.$$
For both flags, $N_B = 0.02 \times 0.9 \times 0.7 = 0.0126$ and $N_G = 0.98 \times 0.06 \times 0.03 = 0.001764$. So
$$\begin{aligned} P(B \mid J \cap V) &= \frac{0.0126}{0.014364} \\ &= \frac{50}{57} \approx 0.877. \end{aligned}$$
Check in odds: $\tfrac{1}{49} \times 15 \times \tfrac{70}{3} = \tfrac{50}{7}$, and odds of $50 : 7$ are a chance of $\tfrac{50}{57}$.

**4. A shared stale quote.** The good-tick part of the assumption fails. On good ticks $V$ happens only together with $J$, so $J \cap V$ is the event $V$ there: $P(J \cap V \mid G) = f_V = 0.03$, not $f_J f_V = 0.0018$. The bad-tick part still holds, so $N_B = 0.0126$ as before, while $N_G = 0.98 \times 0.03 = 0.0294$. So
$$\begin{aligned} P(B \mid J \cap V) &= \frac{0.0126}{0.0126 + 0.0294} \\ &= \frac{0.0126}{0.042} = \frac{3}{10}. \end{aligned}$$
Read as a second update: once $J$ has flagged a good tick, $V$ follows with chance $\tfrac{0.03}{0.06} = 0.5$. So $V$ multiplies the odds after $J$ by $\tfrac{0.7}{0.5} = 1.4$, not $\tfrac{70}{3}$: from $\tfrac{15}{49}$ to $\tfrac{3}{7}$, a chance of $\tfrac{3}{10}$. The second flag moves the view only from 0.234 to 0.3.

rubric.text: Tick only if all are given: $P(B \mid J) = P(J \mid B)\,P(B)/P(J)$ obtained from the multiplication rule, each line with its reason; $P(J) > 0$ named as needed; and $P(J) = h_J b + f_J(1 - b)$ by adding the bad and good cases.

Tick only if all are given: $P(B \mid J \cap V) = \dfrac{h_J h_V b}{h_J h_V b + f_J f_V(1 - b)}$, or prior odds times both likelihood ratios; the assumption in two parts, independent flags on bad ticks and on good ticks; and where each part is used.
$P(B \mid J) = \tfrac{15}{64} \approx 0.234$ and $P(B \mid J \cap V) = \tfrac{50}{57} \approx 0.877$, by any route.
Tick only if all are given: the good-tick part named as the one that fails; $P(J \cap V \mid G) = 0.03$; and $P(B \mid J \cap V) = \tfrac{3}{10}$ by any route.
Checks a two-flag answer by a second route: odds form, a count of imagined ticks, or the one-flag answer updated by the venue flag.
